reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone / Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
clinicalPearls: A benign, slow-growing fibroelastic lesion arising almost exclusively deep to the scapula between the chest wall and the lower scapular tip
Typically occurs in older adults, more often women, and is frequently bilateral
Associated with repetitive manual work and mechanical friction of the scapula against the ribs
Presents as a firm, ill-defined mass that may cause a snapping or clicking sensation with shoulder movement
Characteristic location and imaging appearance often allow a confident diagnosis without biopsy
Histology shows collagen intermixed with abnormal, fragmented, beaded elastic fibres that are highlighted by elastic stains
Asymptomatic lesions can be observed, with marginal excision reserved for symptomatic cases
reference.pathophysiology: Elastofibroma dorsi is a benign fibroelastic proliferation widely regarded as a reactive, degenerative process rather than a true neoplasm. Chronic mechanical friction between the inferior scapula and the underlying rib cage is thought to induce abnormal production and degeneration of elastic fibres within a dense collagenous stroma. The result is a poorly circumscribed mass characterised by numerous swollen, fragmented and beaded elastic fibres admixed with collagen and entrapped fat. Its stereotyped deep periscapular location reflects this mechanical aetiology.
additionalDifferentials: Soft-tissue sarcoma of the chest wall or back
additionalInvestigations: MRI showing a lens-shaped mass with alternating fibrous and fatty signal in the classic periscapular location
CT to demonstrate the characteristic location and internal fat streaks
Ultrasound to confirm the deep subscapular position and layered appearance
Elastic-fibre stains on histology to highlight fragmented beaded elastic fibres if biopsied
Bilateral imaging assessment given the frequency of contralateral lesions
redFlags: Atypical location outside the classic periscapular region
Rapid growth or invasive features suggesting an alternative diagnosis
New neurological or vascular symptoms from local compression
Uncertain imaging appearance prompting histological confirmation
reference.prognosis: Elastofibroma dorsi is entirely benign with no malignant potential, and observation is appropriate for asymptomatic lesions. Marginal excision is curative for symptomatic disease, and recurrence is rare.
pitfalls: Overinvestigating or resecting an asymptomatic lesion with a classic appearance
Mistaking the mass for a sarcoma when the typical location is not recognised
Omitting elastic stains when histological confirmation is sought
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
